doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: First record date with Kai Winding, Shelly Manne and Allen Eager
summary: His first professional date, arranged by Teddy Reig, was tense because of Allen Eager and ran overnight.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: When was your first opportunity to record?

I think the first, well the first professional record date I did was I was working at Childs’ Paramount Restaurant on Broadway and 43rd Street. It was downstairs from the Paramount Theater. Do you remember the Paramount Theater where Frank Sinatra had that whole thing with the bobby soxers? There was a restaurant downstairs called Childs’ Paramount, and I was working with Henry’s band, and I got a call from a guy named Teddy Reig, who was a, did you know that name?

Savoy Records, Guild Records, whatever. And he called me and my first record date was, are you ready for this? My first record date, Kay [sic] Winding, or Kai as he was known later, Shelly Manne, Ed Safranski, and Allen, boy, I just drew a blank.

Yes. How did you know that? Well you should know that. And Allen Eager. And what happened was the gig became a fiasco, I hate to say this, but because of Allen Eager. Because he was like a negative personality. Because Kai would say “hey what are we going to play? How about —” And the guys were making suggestions. Like why don’t we play this, why don’t we play this. Everything was said, Allen would say “no man, don’t play that.” So we tried to please him and say “all right we’ll play that.” Nobody really wanted to play the tunes he wanted, but they were trying to appease him. And everybody wound up like this. And I did a three hour interview for Phil Schaap on WKCR. And he played two of those records. I said, “I thought there was only one, called ‘Olgamore.’” He said, “no, there’s another one.” And I listened to it and I said now I know why I don’t have the other one. It’s terrible. You know it was the beginning of the bebop thing and everybody is [scats], with flatted fifths and all that. And it was really terrible. I mean you’ve got great musicians like this. But it wasn’t very good. Plus the fact that there was so much tension at that date. We went in at about one o’clock in the morning and we played until about twelve noon the next day, and they only put that one record out, two sides or whatever it was, and we never got paid for the overtime. So I saw Teddy Reig about 30 years later, I says, “hey Teddy, you know I never got any overtime for that date?” He says, “here, here’s ten dollars.” He gave me ten dollars out of his pocket.
